appraisal_events.evidence: "Bloch voulut faire un geste pour exprimer son admiration, mais d'un coup de coude il renversa le vase où était la branche et toute l'eau se répandit sur le tapis", immediately followed by the historian's oblivious "Vous avez vraiment des doigts de fée" addressed to the marquise, "ne s'était pas aperçu de la maladresse de Bloch".
appraisal_events.explanation: Bloch's imitative bid to join the salon's admiration collapses into a physical blunder, and the narrator sharpens the ridicule by placing the compliment about 'fairy fingers' directly against his clumsiness, which no one even witnesses.

appraisal_events.evidence: "j'ai beau être une vieille dame, je connais du monde, j'ai quelques amis, ajouta-t-elle en souriant par simplicité, crut-on généralement, plutôt, me sembla-t-il, parce qu'elle trouvait du piquant à tirer vanité de l'amitié d'une fleuriste quand on avait d'aussi grandes relations."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator sets his own reading against the room's ('crut-on généralement' versus 'me sembla-t-il') and reclassifies her modesty as an inverted vanity, deflating her self-presentation even as the same sentence confirms that her connections really are grand.

status_effects.explanation: The passage's closing joke is entirely at Bloch's expense: his attempt at a gesture of admiration produces only spilled water on the carpet.
Within the salon he is marked as awkward and out of place, and the blunder passes unnoticed by the guest whose compliment fills the same moment.
She is locally lowered because the narrator exposes her simplicity as a refined form of vanity rather than accepting it at face value.

ambiguities: The historian of the Fronde, who supplies the passage's overt praise of the marquise ('avec un talent pareil et vos cinq langues', 'des doigts de fée'), is descriptor-identified and absent from the reference sheet, so his flattery is recorded only through the narrator's framing; read as ironized courtiership (he compliments with his back turned, oblivious) rather than as a genuine elevation of Mme de Villeparisis.

E2's polarity is genuinely double-edged: the same clause that convicts her of vanity ('quand on avait d'aussi grandes relations') also certifies her social eminence; the reading committed to here treats the narrator's deflation as dominant and the confirmation of rank as its by-product.
